b: Claude Code wraps CLAUDE.md in a reminder saying it may be irrelevant, so the more of it that does not apply to the current task, the likelier the model is to ignore all of it.

a: Wrap domain-specific CLAUDE.md sections in <important if="condition"> blocks so the model gets an explicit relevance signal that overrides the 'may not be relevant' framing, keeping everything inline.
b: Rewrite CLAUDE.md so domain-specific rules sit in inline <important if="specific trigger"> blocks, giving the model an explicit relevance signal instead of sharding into separate files.

a: Keep project identity, project map and tech stack bare at the top; only task-specific guidance gets conditional wrappers (90% relevance rule of thumb).
b: Keep project identity, map and tech stack bare at the top; wrap only guidance relevant to specific kinds of work, and keep all commands.

a: Delete from CLAUDE.md anything a linter, formatter or pre-commit hook can enforce, and suggest pre-push/pre-commit hooks instead.
b: Delete from CLAUDE.md anything a linter/formatter/hook can enforce or the agent can discover from existing code patterns, and suggest pre-push or pre-commit hooks instead.

a: Replace code snippets in CLAUDE.md with file path references; snippets go stale and bloat.
b: Replace code snippets in CLAUDE.md with file-path references, and delete vague instructions like 'follow best practices' that are not concrete and actionable.

a: Avoid progressive disclosure into separate files unless the content is very verbose; conditional inline blocks keep everything visible while weighting what matches, so sharding is a last resort.
b: Against progressive disclosure by default: sharding CLAUDE.md into files the agent must fetch is only justified when the extra context is very verbose; inline-but-conditionally-weighted is preferred.

a: Harness engineering and loops cannot fix models' inability to maintain codebase quality, because that is a training (RL reward) problem.
b: Harness engineering (linters, adversarial review bots, loops) cannot fix a deficiency that comes from how models are trained and benchmarked.

a: More review agents and tokens raise the floor by catching dumb mistakes but do not raise the quality ceiling; a model judging quality is bounded by its training.
b: Review agents and extra tokens raise the quality floor by catching dumb mistakes but do not raise the ceiling, which is set by what RL taught the model about design.

a: Model-as-judge for maintainability is circular: a reliable judge would imply a reliable author.
b: Model-as-judge for code quality is limited: a judge that could tell good design reliably would usually have produced it, and maintainability has no fast oracle.

a: Benchmark graders discard the agent's test-file edits before applying the held-out test patch because models were caught commenting out or mocking failing tests.
b: Benchmark graders discard the agent's edits to test files because models game tests by disabling them or mocking them; a grader must run held-out tests.

a: Quality verification is far harder than pass/fail because bad-design cost shows up weeks or months later and cannot be backpropagated to the decision.
b: Verification of test passing is seconds-fast while the cost of bad architecture shows up in weeks to years, so fast loops reward the wrong thing.

a: Agent-built codebases start to slow and need a different approach to adding features after roughly three to six months, making 'brownfield' arrive much sooner.
b: An agent-built codebase starts to slow down after roughly three to six months, and the way new work is added has to change.

a: When agents build in minutes, human review becomes the bottleneck; adding agentic review and regression testing helps but review remains the constraint.
b: When agents cut build time to minutes, human review becomes the bottleneck; agentic review and regression testing speed it up but review likely stays the constraint.

a: Mock up UI as rough HTML instead of describing it; a mockup settles arguments that paragraphs prolong.
b: For product alignment, mock up the actual screen as rough HTML plus a JSON outline of the feature instead of describing it in prose.

a: Author-opt-in review: the author picks the eventual PR reviewer and walks through product/tech specs with them before coding, asynchronously via doc comments or live.
b: Author-opt-in review: the author picks the eventual PR reviewer and walks through the product and tech specs with them (async doc comments) before any code is written.

a: Program design: before implementation, agree types, method signatures, program layout and call stacks, drafted by the model and argued by the human, so decisions are made before review.
b: Before implementation, write the shape of the code: types, method signatures, program layout and call stacks; each is a decision otherwise made implicitly at review time, the most expensive time to change your mind.

a: Models plan in stack order (migrations, service, API, frontend) so nothing can be touched until the end; prefer vertical slices (tracer bullets) starting in the middle with mock data and curl/browser checks at each step.
b: Models default to horizontal plans (migrations, services, API, frontend in order) that can't be touched until the end; vertical slices (tracer bullets) let you curl or open the browser at each step.

a: Review code at each slice (100-200 lines) when quality matters, and send the agent off on only 1-3 slices at a time rather than reviewing 2k+ lines at once.
b: Review each step in 100-200 line increments and resteer early; send a model off for 1-3 slices at a time rather than reaching 2k+ lines with no idea what is broken.

a: Task-size routing: about 40% of tasks are oneshot; medium tasks get product/system design in one plan doc with no phases; large tasks get all steps (product skipped for refactors).
b: Task routing by size: about 40% oneshot; medium tasks get product and system design in one plan doc without phasing; large tasks get every step, skipping product for refactors.

a: PRs needing 20% rework (AI oneshot PRs closer to 50%) burden submitter and reviewer; a good PR is quick to review.
b: The PR overload is a rework problem: a great PR is a joy to review, whereas 20% rework (he estimates AI oneshot PRs trend closer to 50%) is a heavy burden for submitter and reviewer.

a: Closing stance: accept the constraints, aim for 2-3x not 10-100x, learn model constraints by use, seek leverage, and read the code.
b: Accept that models are good at some things and not others, move 2-3x faster safely rather than chase 10-100x, and close with: learn the constraints, optimise within them, seek leverage, read the code.

a: HumanLayer positions itself around 'building blocks for your software factory' and 'better verifiers for software maintainability', treating verifier quality as the missing piece.
b: HumanLayer's product direction is two ideas: building blocks for a software factory, and better verifiers for software maintainability (possibly better models).

a: A Faros AI report shows after AI tool adoption: longer and more comments, many PRs merged with no review, more incidents and more bugs per developer; he calls it correlation, not proof.

a: Step D (design discussion, ~200 lines): current state, desired end state, patterns to follow, resolved decisions and open questions in one editable markdown artifact.
b: Planning is split into a design discussion (current state, desired end state, patterns to follow, open questions; about 200 lines) and a structure outline (phases and checkpoints), mapping to design review and sprint planning.

a: Rank the worst context failures as incorrect information first, missing information second, noise third; optimise for correctness, completeness, size, trajectory.
b: Context should be optimised for correctness, completeness, size and trajectory, ranked by harm: wrong info worst, then missing info, then noise.

a: The design doc is the cheap place to steer the agent: have it brain-dump its understanding and the patterns it found, and correct bad-pattern choices before any code exists.
b: Reviewing the design doc before planning lets you correct the model's understanding cheaply, instead of re-steering after code exists.

a: Use the stronger model for research and planning and a cheaper model to implement each plan phase.
b: Route the stronger model to codebase research and planning and the cheaper model to implementation.

a: Agents read the repository and imitate its patterns, so one poor decision becomes precedent and precedent becomes architecture; slop compounds.

a: A staged up-front chain (product review, architecture, program design, vertical slices) cuts review time and makes reading every line feasible.

a: Never filter test output through head/tail/grep; rely on the Bash tool spooling long output to a persisted file and grep that file, so a long test run is never re-run just to see different lines.
